title: Units, Dimensions and Vectors — Class 12 NIOS Physics
subject: Physics

slides.title: Units, Dimensions and Vectors
bullets: Class 12 — NIOS Physics
Chapter 1
slides.speaker_notes: Welcome students. This is a foundational chapter. Every later chapter relies on the SI system, dimensional analysis as a sanity check, and the vector vocabulary we set up here.

slides.title: What you'll be able to do
bullets: List the seven SI base units and identify common derived units.
Write the dimensional formula of a quantity and check the consistency of an equation.
Compute mean / relative / percentage errors and propagate them.
Distinguish scalars from vectors and resolve a vector into components.
Compute scalar (dot) and vector (cross) products and apply them.
slides.speaker_notes: Read each objective; ask students which they feel least sure about.

slides.title: Physical quantities and SI units
bullets: A measurement = numerical value + unit.
Seven SI base units: m, kg, s, A, K, mol, cd.
Derived units: N (force), J (energy), W (power), Pa (pressure), Hz (frequency), C (charge).
Decimal prefixes scale across many orders: n, μ, m, k, M, G.
Convention is everything: 1 km = 10³ m; 1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m.
slides.speaker_notes: Make sure students see that 'force' is derived (N = kg·m/s²) — a common source of confusion in board-exam mistakes.

slides.title: Dimensions and dimensional analysis
bullets: Dimensions express how a quantity depends on M, L, T, A.
Force [M L T⁻²]; energy [M L² T⁻²]; pressure [M L⁻¹ T⁻²].
Principle of homogeneity: every term in a valid equation has the same dimensions.
Used for (i) consistency checks, (ii) deriving formulas, (iii) unit conversions.
Limitations: cannot fix dimensionless constants or functional forms.
slides.speaker_notes: Pause on limitations — students often think dimensional analysis can do more than it actually can.

slides.title: Worked example: derive T for a pendulum
bullets: Assume T = k L^a g^b.
Match dimensions: T¹ = L^(a+b) T^(−2b).
Hence T ∝ √(L/g); the constant 2π comes from physics, not dimensions.
slides.speaker_notes: Walk slowly; ask students to call out each step. Stress the role of physics vs dimensions.

slides.title: Significant figures and errors
bullets: Sig figs: meaningful digits in a measurement.
Multiply / divide → match sig figs to least precise input.
Add / subtract → match decimal places.
Errors: systematic, random, gross.
Combining: products add relative errors; sums add absolute errors; powers multiply by exponent.
slides.speaker_notes: Demo the difference: 12.45 + 1.2 = 13.7 (one decimal), but 3.45 × 2.0 = 6.9 (2 sig figs).

slides.title: Error propagation example
bullets: Sphere radius r = 2.00 ± 0.01 cm.
Volume V = (4/3) π r³.
Rule: relative error in xⁿ is n × (relative error in x).
So small errors in r blow up in derived quantities like volume.
slides.speaker_notes: Stress that ± 0.5% in a radius becomes ± 1.5% in the volume. This 'amplification' is why error propagation matters in practice.

slides.title: Scalars and vectors
bullets: Scalar: magnitude + unit (mass, energy, time).
Vector: magnitude + direction (displacement, velocity, force).
Vectors are equal iff same magnitude AND same direction.
Unit vectors î, ĵ, k̂ along +x, +y, +z (each magnitude 1).
Special types: zero, equal, negative, collinear, coplanar.
slides.speaker_notes: Use arrow diagrams on the board; emphasise that the position of the tail does NOT matter.

slides.title: Resolving a vector
bullets: A force of 50 N acts at 53° above +x axis.
Take cos 53° ≈ 0.6 and sin 53° ≈ 0.8.
So \vec{F} = 30 î + 40 ĵ N.
slides.speaker_notes: After the example, ask 'What is |F| from the components?' to reinforce √(30² + 40²) = 50.

slides.title: Vector products
bullets: Dot product: \vec{a} · \vec{b} = a b cos θ → SCALAR.
Cross product: \vec{a} × \vec{b} → VECTOR with |·| = a b sin θ.
Direction by right-hand rule, perpendicular to both.
Dot product zero ⇔ vectors perpendicular.
Cross product zero ⇔ vectors parallel.
slides.speaker_notes: Use the right-hand-rule demo: point fingers from a to b; thumb shows direction of a × b.

slides.title: Two physics applications
bullets: Work done by a constant force: W = \vec{F} · \vec{d}.
Torque: \vec{τ} = \vec{r} × \vec{F}.
Work uses dot (along-direction), torque uses cross (perpendicular).
If \vec{F} ⊥ \vec{d}, no work is done.
If \vec{F} ∥ \vec{r}, no torque is exerted.
slides.speaker_notes: Tie the abstract products to physical pictures students can visualise — pushing a box along a floor (dot) vs turning a wrench (cross).

slides.title: You try (5 minutes)
bullets: 1. Find the dimensional formula of momentum.
2. Compute (3î + 4ĵ) · (4î − 3ĵ).
3. Find a unit vector along 5î + 12ĵ.
4. State two limitations of dimensional analysis.
Compare answers with your bench partner.
slides.speaker_notes: Walk the room. Watch for students forgetting the magnitude in question 3.

slides.title: Quick check
bullets: Q1. Is force a fundamental SI quantity?
Q2. Dimensions of energy?
Q3. Magnitude of a sum of two perpendicular vectors of magnitudes 6 and 8?
Q4. Dot product of perpendicular vectors?
Show your answers on fingers.
slides.speaker_notes: Use show-of-fingers to gauge the room. Address the question with the most disagreement.

slides.title: Key takeaways
bullets: SI base units anchor every measurement.
Every valid equation passes the dimensional homogeneity check.
Sig figs and error propagation tell you how trustworthy your answer is.
Vectors require both magnitude and direction.
Dot gives a scalar (a b cos θ); cross gives a vector (a b sin θ, perpendicular by right-hand rule).
slides.speaker_notes: End with the 5 takeaways. Hand out the worksheet and announce the homework prompts.
